text: Hooper House II is a house in Baltimore, commissioned by the philanthropist Edith Hooper and designed by Marcel Breuer with Herbert Beckhard. Ground was broken in 1958 and the house was finished in 1959. Its plan is binuclear: a central courtyard splits the house into two parts, one for living, dining, cooking and entertaining, the other for the family and bedrooms. The front door faces this courtyard, and glass doors and a large rectangular opening in the stone rear wall frame a clear view right through the house to Lake Roland. Thick stone walls help control noise. Almost every room sits on the edge of the plan with a full wall of glass, half of it sliding doors. The lake side is glazed, while the west side is a long, almost blank wall of Maryland fieldstone.

Teatro Oficina is the home of a São Paulo theatre company founded in 1958 at the Law School of the University of São Paulo. After a fire destroyed the company's headquarters in 1966, revivals of its plays raised money to restore the building. The present theatre was designed in 1984 by Lina Bo Bardi and Edson Elito and opened in 1994. Its main move is a central walkway 1.5 metres wide and 50 metres long, with entrances at both front and back. The design combines iron scaffolding, an exposed brick structure, planting beds and a large window. In 2015 The Guardian named it the best theatre in the world for architectural design. Since the 1980s the company has been in a dispute with Grupo Silvio Santos over residential towers planned on the land next door.

Kiyonori Kikutake built the Sky House in Tokyo in 1958 as his own home. It stands on a hillside as a raised platform carried by four concrete panels and covered by a hyperbolic paraboloid shell roof. Inside is one single space, divided only by storage units, with the kitchen and bathroom placed on the outer edge. These two parts were designed so they could be moved to suit the way the house was used. Kikutake developed it with the structural engineer Gengo Matsui, his partner on more than 40 buildings. Kenzo Tange presented the house, together with Kikutake's Tower-shaped City, at CIAM '59 in Otterlo, the last CIAM meeting. After his 13 May lecture, Louis Kahn was invited to the house and talked at length there with Japanese architects, including the Metabolists.

The Fredensborg Houses are a housing estate in Denmark that Jørn Utzon designed for Danes who had spent long periods working abroad. Dansk Samvirke invited him to create a place where returning pensioners could live together and share their experiences. The scheme grew from a 1953 competition project, inspired by Danish farmhouses set around a courtyard and by Chinese architecture: each home opens onto a central court but is shielded from the outside by its outer wall. Utzon worked additively, starting with one unit and growing from it while following the lie of the land. The estate mixes courtyard homes and terraced houses with a central building holding a restaurant, meeting rooms and guest rooms. On a slope and facing south-east or south-west, the houses all get plenty of light. The additive approach influenced later housing.

Baker House is a co-ed student dormitory at MIT, at 362 Memorial Drive in Cambridge, designed by the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto in 1947–1948 and built in 1949, after he returned to MIT following the Second World War. The building runs alongside the Charles River, and its undulating form gives each resident the greatest possible view and ventilation. It was the first building of Aalto's red-brick period. He used brick here to signal the Ivy League university tradition, then went on to use it in a number of key buildings back in Finland, most notably several at the new Helsinki University of Technology. For its fiftieth anniversary in 1999 the dormitory was renovated: plumbing, telecommunications and electrical systems were modernised, and some later interior changes that were not part of Aalto's original design were removed.

Cocoa House is a skyscraper in Dugbe, a major commercial area of Ibadan, Nigeria, designed by The Plan Group (West Africa). Chief Obafemi Awolowo initiated it in the late 1950s as part of the Western Region Development Plan, and it was first named Ìlé Àwọn Àgbẹ̀, or "House of Farmers". It was paid for from the region's farm produce, such as cocoa, rubber and timber. It was renamed Cocoa House because cocoa exports funded it and a cocoa tree was planted in front, beside a fountain. Completed in July 1964 and commissioned in July 1965, it rises 105 metres and was the first skyscraper in West Africa, and Nigeria's tallest building until 1979. A fire gutted it in January 1985; after renovation it reopened for commercial use in 1992 and now holds offices for major firms and broadcasting companies.

BedZED, the Beddington Zero Energy Development, is an environmentally friendly housing scheme in Hackbridge, London. The architect Bill Dunster designed it to be carbon neutral. Built between 2000 and 2002, it holds 82 homes and 1,405 square metres of work space. It was the first construction project where a local authority sold land below market value so that sustainable development could pay its way. Electricity use came to 3 kilowatt hours per person per day, 25% below the UK average, and 11% of that came from solar panels. Not everything worked: the "Living Machine" water recycling facility could not clean the water well enough. BedZED was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003, and the judges of the RIBA Journal sustainability award praised it for challenging the way people both live and work.

Crow Island School in Winnetka, Illinois, serves children from kindergarten to fourth grade. It was designed jointly by the Chicago firm Perkins, Wheeler & Will with Eliel and Eero Saarinen and established in 1940–41. Known for its progressive philosophy, it was one of the first North American schools in the International Style. First, the architects interviewed students and teachers and sat in on classes. The site, Crow Island, is a high spot in the Skokie Marsh, filled with landfill from two Works Progress Administration projects. Four wings branch out from a central block of common rooms, so every classroom has its own outdoor courtyard. The single storey is flat except for a 15-metre chimney on the north face, a vertical "fifth wing". It won the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award in 1971 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1990.

Charles and Ray Eames built this mid-century modern house in Los Angeles in 1949 for themselves. It was part of the Case Study House program, announced by John Entenza in Arts & Architecture magazine in 1945. With Eero Saarinen, the couple first proposed a raised, L-shaped structure, then reworked it into two separate rectangular pavilions, a residence and a studio, built of various materials. As House 8 in the program, it was completely redesigned from its original plan, for reasons still disputed. Work began in 1948, and the frame went up in a day and a half in 1949. The residence lies to the south of a central courtyard and the studio to the north. Both pavilions sit on a hillside along the western edge of the site, leaving the rest to trees and a meadow.

Eastgate Centre is a shopping centre and office block in central Harare, Zimbabwe, designed by Mick Pearce and built by Ove Arup and Partners. Pearce took his cue from the termite mound, which keeps a constant temperature despite large swings between night and day. Nine storeys of commercial space run in two rows along a glass-covered atrium, with shops on the first two floors and offices above. Forty-eight brick funnels link to every office and shop, drawing cool air from the basement and letting hot air out at the top. The passive system gathers cool night air and spreads it through the interior by day, while massive concrete walls cut solar heat gain. The masonry patterns recall the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe. It is reported to use just 10% of the energy of a similar conventionally cooled building.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this house, built 1946–1948, for the journalist Herbert Jacobs and his wife Katherine, whose first house he had designed a decade earlier. The name comes from its semicircular-arc plan, natural materials and energy-saving orientation. The Jacobses turned down his first scheme, and this second one is partly sunk into an earthen berm. The north side is built into the berm, with a round, stone-faced stair tower; to the south, a curved glass wall faces a sunken garden. A tunnel through the berm leads in. Above the berm, a narrow band of clerestory windows brings light and summer air into the rear. Limestone slabs laid horizontally, alternately pushed out and set back, read like natural outcrops. After contractor delays and a misunderstanding that led Wright to resign, the Jacobses built much of it themselves.

Spa Green Estate stands between Rosebery Avenue and St John Street in Clerkenwell, London. Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton first designed it in 1938 and developed it in 1943, and it is seen as the most complete post-war realisation of a 1930s plan for social renewal through Modernist architecture. Lubetkin meant it as a manifesto, rational but exciting: "we will deliberately create exhilaration". It brought features of his luxury Highpoint flats to working families, including lifts, central heating, balconies, a roof terrace, and daylight and air from several sides. Ove Arup's concrete box-frame, or "egg-crate", construction gave each flat clear views and rooms free of beams, columns and pipes. Two parallel eight-storey blocks frame a plaza with a nursery school, while Sadler House curves along the edge. Listed Grade II* in 1998, it had its original colours restored in 2008.

The entrances to the Bilbao Metro, known as "fosteritos", are glass structures named after their designer, Norman Foster. Foster and partners won the design of the underground stations in an open competition in 1988, and the system opened in 1995. Below ground, each station is dug as a large cavern with a cross-section of 160 square metres, giving one big open space instead of the usual chain of linked tunnels. The ticket area shares this volume with the trains, on steel "mezzanines" built over the tracks, and lifts and escalators make the trains fully accessible. Steel and concrete are used throughout. Sarriko station breaks the pattern: in place of a fosterito, a vast glazed atrium floods the whole station with daylight, above a long, unbroken escalator ride from the street to the ticket hall. It won the 1998 Brunel Award for Railway Design.

Built for the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the Mesa Laboratory sits on the Table Mesa below the Flatirons sandstone cliffs in Boulder. I. M. Pei designed it in 1961, his first project outside city building design. He based it on the Anasazi cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, using geometric forms, bush-hammered concrete and a local pinkish aggregate so the complex blends into the hills. Through his revisions, a single tall tower became a village-like group of three five-storey towers, built in two phases to suit a budget set by the National Science Foundation. The plan is laid out like a maze to encourage scientists to meet. Completed in 1966 and dedicated in 1967, it suffered leaky roofs and problems with the flow of people, yet won the 1967 Laboratory of the Year award and, in 1997, the AIA Colorado chapter's 25 Year Award. As of 2009 it remained NCAR's main laboratory.

Diamond Ranch High School sits on a steep hillside in Pomona, on land once thought unusable. It was designed in an expressionist modern style by Morphosis and Thomas Blurock Architects, with Thom Mayne of Morphosis leading the work. The project began with a vote: in June 1991 district voters approved a $62.5 million bond to improve schools, with about $10 million set aside for Diamond Ranch. The district hired Morphosis in November 1993, and the school opened to students on 5 September 1997 while construction was still going on. Its design is the subject of the book Morphosis/Diamond Ranch High School. Because of its modernist architecture, size and setting in California, the campus has appeared in films including The Cell, Orange County, Serenity, Live Free or Die Hard and The Thinning.

The Binoculars Building in Los Angeles began as the Chiat/Day Building, built in 1991 for the advertising agency Chiat/Day and designed by Frank Gehry. Its popular name comes from Giant Binoculars, a 1991 public artwork by the artists Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen, set on the street-facing facade. The sculpture is more than decoration: it covers both a car entrance and a pedestrian entrance, and the way into the parking garage runs between its two telescopes. Work on the building, about 7,000 square metres in size, was delayed for a few years after hazardous materials were found on the site and had to be removed. In 2011 Google became the tenant and added two neighbouring buildings as part of a major expansion to build a larger workforce in Los Angeles.

Solar do Unhão is the main cultural centre of Salvador, Brazil. It was once a sugar mill, named after the 17th-century Brazilian high court judge Pedro Unhão Castelo Branco. When the governor of Bahia invited Lina Bo Bardi to direct a new art museum in the North East of Brazil, she was commissioned to turn the mill into a museum of modern art, built between 1959 and 1963. Her aim was to restore old buildings without either giving in to nostalgia or ignoring their context, so she kept the colonial exterior intact and added a modern staircase. She wanted the museum to show the primitive art of the North East and the practical nature of its design. For Bo Bardi a museum was not a mausoleum of the past but an active place of knowledge, and in its early years it ran many classes in art and history for local people.

Completed in 2001, Gando Primary School was the first school in Gando, Burkina Faso, and Diébédo Francis Kéré's first building. To pay for it he set up the association Schulbausteine für Gando, "Building Blocks for Gando", now the Kéré Foundation. Schools in Burkina Faso are usually built of concrete, which is costly and turns intolerably hot inside. Kéré chose local earth instead, made into mud bricks. A wide, raised tin roof keeps rain off the walls and lets air move beneath it to cool the building. He drew early plans in the sand for villagers, many of whom could not read, and they joined in fully. His aim was to combine what he had learned in Europe with traditional building methods. The school won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2004. A library added in 2012, again built with local help, has dozens of bottomless clay pots set into its roof to light the reading room.

The Salk Institute stands on the Torrey Pines Mesa in La Jolla, on land San Diego granted after Jonas Salk and Louis Kahn asked for it in March 1960 and a referendum approved it that June. Salk wanted a beautiful campus to draw the best researchers in the world. Kahn planned three clusters, for meetings, living and laboratories, but only the laboratories were built: two parallel, symmetric wings either side of a travertine-paved plaza. A thin linear fountain runs down the middle towards the ocean, framing a long view of the Pacific. After two years of design, Kahn and the Institute switched from four narrow laboratory buildings of two floors to two wider ones of three. No walls divide the laboratories on any floor, to encourage collaboration. August Komendant re-engineered the structure and trained the builders to produce a highly refined concrete finish.

This chapel in Pampulha, Belo Horizonte, was designed by Oscar Niemeyer in the organic modern style, with the city's mayor, Juscelino Kubitschek, as patron. Here Niemeyer left behind slabs on columns and built a parabolic concrete vault, a form used until then only for hangars. Four undulating concrete parabolas serve as both structure and enclosure, so no masonry walls are needed. Outside, pastel ceramic tiles in light blue and white form abstract designs, with art panels by Candido Portinari and Paulo Werneck; inside are Portinari's Stations of the Cross in 14 panels. Roberto Burle Marx designed the landscape. Although finished in 1943, the church was not consecrated until 1959, because church authorities barred Catholic services there for 14 years. It is the first listed modern architectural monument in Brazil.

Giancarlo De Carlo designed this neighbourhood in Terni between 1969 and 1974 to house 3,000 workers of the company Società Terni Acciaierie. Built in concrete in a New Brutalist manner, it is known for the large part its future residents played in the design, an example of participatory design. More than a thousand people took part in meetings, interviews and debates, and in 1970 an exhibition of housing models from around the world showed the community what was possible. The houses vary in size and are tied together by a web of stairs, corridors and gardens. De Carlo saw the project as a test of his theory of popular participation and as an answer to Carlo Aymonino's Monte Amiata housing in Milan. Yet he wanted to set a low-rise, high-density plan, while the sociologist De Mesi wanted residents involved in every part. Opposition from the old village and the company president's departure left it only partly built.

The Michael Lee-Chin Crystal is the centrepiece of the Royal Ontario Museum's expansion in Toronto, a deconstructivist structure with a crystalline form. Daniel Libeskind's design was chosen from 50 finalists in an international competition, and the Crystal opened in 2007 in place of the Queen Elizabeth II Terrace Galleries, with a new sliding-door entrance on Bloor Street. Its canted walls stop short of the existing heritage buildings and are used to close the envelope between the new form and the old walls. The main lobby is a three-storey atrium, the Hyacinth Gloria Chen Crystal Court. The Crystal also holds seven more galleries, a cafeteria, a gift shop and Canada's largest temporary exhibition hall in a museum. Its design is close to other Libeskind works, notably the Jewish Museum in Berlin. The addition was controversial, and in October 2007 it was reported to be leaking significantly.

Luis Barragán lived in this Mexico City house until his death in 1988, altering it many times so that it worked as a laboratory for his ideas. The street front is plain: the facades line up with the road, and their rough cement walls are close in colour and texture to the neighbours. The house turns inward instead, centred on a garden enclosed by high walls on every side but the west. Floor levels vary and rooms have different heights. Apart from the breakfast nook, no room needs artificial light by day, because windows and openings are placed to admit as much light as possible. The colours draw on the bright tones of traditional Mexico, tempered by the artists Rufino Tamayo and Jesús Reyes Ferreira. Its influences are mostly Mexican, with some international ones. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2004 as one of the most influential and representative works of modern Mexican architecture.

Bloomberg London was designed by Foster and Partners with the structural engineer AKT II and built by Sir Robert McAlpine at a cost of £1bn. It is made of two buildings split by a covered arcade and joined by bridges; the arcade holds restaurants and brings back part of Watling Street, an ancient Roman road. The facades are clad in 9,600 tonnes of Derbyshire sandstone with bronze ventilation fins. The cores sit on the outside to free a single open-plan space within. Inside, custom glass lifts and a 210-metre helical bronze ramp tie the floors together. The lobby is a self-supporting "vortex" of three curved timber shells, from which express lifts rise to a double-height pantry on the sixth floor with a view of St Paul's Cathedral. It scored 98.5% under the BREEAM sustainability assessment, the highest design-stage score ever achieved by a major office development.

Opened in 1967 with a concert conducted by Benjamin Britten, the Queen Elizabeth Hall is a South Bank music venue in London, built with the smaller Purcell Room as part of the Southbank Centre. The two auditoriums came from a Greater London Council team led by Hubert Bennett, with Jack Whittle, F. G. West and Geoffrey Horsefall. Rather than compete with the scale of the neighbouring Royal Festival Hall, the design breaks the building into separate masses. A vee-shaped foyer sits at first-floor level on octagonal reinforced concrete columns, joined to the auditorium by concrete tubes that recall a spaceship's docking gear. The auditorium is its own building, its seating cantilevered towards the foyer on a massive column that holds the escape stairs. With minimal decoration, it is brutalist work that draws out the plasticity of concrete.

John Lautner designed this modernist house in Los Angeles in 1960 for a site so steep, with a 45-degree slope, that it was thought practically unbuildable. His answer was a one-storey octagon of around 2,200 square feet perched on a concrete column about 1.5 metres wide and nearly 9 metres high. A buried concrete pedestal almost 6 metres across holds the column, and the house has come through earthquakes and heavy rain. A funicular carries people up to it. Inside, a central wall of exposed brick with a fireplace splits the plan in two. The client, aerospace engineer Leonard Malin, had been given the lot by his father-in-law and had limited means, so the cost was partly covered by barter with two sponsors; one of them, Chem Seal, supplied experimental coatings and resins and gave the house its name.

Popularly called 'The Pot', this Rotterdam building is an art depot for Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, designed by the Dutch firm MVRDV and described as the first publicly accessible art depot in the world. Its form is a bowl 39.5 metres high, inspired by an aluminium-coloured IKEA bowl, and its surface is covered in almost continuous reflective plates that give back a reduced mirror image of the surroundings. On the side facing the neighbouring Erasmus MC hospital, some plates are matt to protect patients' privacy. Inside, more than 151,000 objects are kept in fourteen storage compartments with five different climates. The museum's previous storage space flooded severely in 2013, which pushed the idea of an open depot where the public can see work not on show in the main museum.

On the north bank of the River Liffey, Dublin's Custom House is an 18th-century neoclassical building that now houses the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. The project was the idea of John Beresford, who became Ireland's first commissioner of revenue in 1780. After the original architect, Thomas Cooley, died, Beresford appointed James Gandon in 1781, giving him his first large-scale commission. The scheme met strong opposition: Dublin Corporation and some merchants said it shifted the city's axis, left little room for shipping and stood on swampy ground, and a mob of several thousand disrupted the foundations. Beresford pressed on. Gandon chose Irish craftsmen as assistants, among them stone-cutter Henry Darley, and every available mason in the city joined the work. Coats-of-arms and sculptures by Edward Smyth representing Ireland's rivers decorate all four facades.

In Hamar, Norway, the Hedmark Museum is a regional museum whose grounds include the medieval Cathedral Ruins mentioned in Sigrid Undset's Kristin Lavransdatter. Its main building, Storhamarlåven, began as a barn built beside the ruins in the 17th century for the Storhamar farm. Sverre Fehn reworked it in concrete, wood and glass, materials chosen to contrast with the stone of the medieval remains. His aim was to bring out both layers of history: the medieval structure and the later farm building. Ramps carry visitors up so they can view the museum from above. The design won the Betongtavlen architectural award in 1976. The cathedral ruins themselves now sit under a glass shelter by Lund & Slaatto Architects, completed in 1998.

Built in 1895 in Brussels, the Villa Bloemenwerf was the home of the Belgian painter, architect and interior designer Henry van de Velde, and his first work as an architect. He designed the house, its interiors and its furniture, drawing partly on William Morris's Red House in Bexleyheath. His reach went further still: he created textiles, wallpaper, silverware and even clothing to match the style of the house. His wife, Maria Sèthe, designed the garden around it. Besides being the family home, the villa served as a workshop for van de Velde and his collaborators and as a meeting place for the European intellectual and artistic elite of the time. For students it is a compact case of one designer shaping every scale, from the building down to the objects and clothes used inside it.

Walter Gropius planned this building in Dessau as the school of the Bauhaus School of Art, Design and Architecture, and it was built between 1925 and 1926. Its reinforced concrete-frame wings are laid out on a flat site so that there is no 'front' in the usual sense. By setting the support columns back from the edge, Gropius could run an unbroken glass facade across all three floors and the full length of the building. That delicate steel-framed glass skin also caused major problems with sun protection and with controlling the indoor climate. The building was restored and partly modernised in 1976, then restored and repaired again between 1996 and 2006 following the principles of historic preservation. Since 1996 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Bauhaus and its Sites.

SANAA's urban campus in Milan is an expansion of Bocconi University, holding the new seat of the SDA Bocconi School of Management, a student dorm and a sports centre with an Olympic-size swimming pool. The Japanese firm gave the buildings sinuous volumes and facades, glazed ground floors and interior courtyards. Those courtyards draw on a feature typical of Milanese architecture, and together with the glass at street level they make the complex porous to the public. Gardens separate the buildings, and sheltered porticoes link them, so people can cross between them under cover. The project is a useful study in how a university complex can stay open to the city around it: soft forms, a transparent base and covered routes all work to keep its edges permeable rather than closed.

Phoenix's Burton Barr Central Library is a five-storey building that opened in May 1995, designed as a collaboration between DWL Architects and Will Bruder. It covers 280,000 square feet. At its centre is an open core with three high-speed elevators and a five-level grand staircase known as the 'crystal canyon', which carries people up through the building. The roof structure was inspired by Buckminster Fuller's tensegrity structures. Each long facade meets the sun differently: shade sails line the north side, while motorised louvres on the south give better sun control. Daylight is also staged with care. At solar noon, some of the roof skylights cast circles of sunlight straight down the library's north-south midline, a few of them reaching the ground-floor lobby. The building shows how structure, climate and light can be designed together.

Set in a reclaimed china clay pit at Bodelva in Cornwall, the Eden Project by Nicholas Grimshaw is a visitor attraction dominated by two huge enclosures of adjoining domes. Each enclosure recreates a natural biome, one a rainforest and the other a Mediterranean environment, and together they house thousands of plant species. The structure is light: hundreds of hexagonal and pentagonal cells of inflated ETFE, carried by geodesic domes of tubular steel. The idea dates from 1996, and construction began in 1998. Building in the pit was hard. It lies 15 metres below the water table, and torrential rain in the first months of work flooded parts of it. For students of high-tech design, it shows how a repeated geometry and a thin membrane can enclose very large planted spaces on difficult ground.

Carlo Scarpa worked on the Brion Cemetery in San Vito d'Altivole from 1968 to 1978, shaping an L-shaped extension of about 2,000 square metres beside the municipal cemetery. It was commissioned in 1969 by Onorina Tomasin-Brion, widow of Giuseppe Brion, founder of the Brionvega company, as a private burial ground. Scarpa believed that 'the place for the dead is a garden', and the design follows that idea: concrete buildings with carefully worked detailing sit among gardens and water. The influences are layered. Gold tiles recall Byzantine mosaics familiar from Venice, while the chapel takes its inspiration from the Japanese tea room. Scarpa himself is buried next to the Brion sanctuary. A conservation restoration of the tomb was completed in September 2021. It is a rich study in how detail, water and planting can carry the meaning of a memorial.

The Seoul branch of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art opened on 13 November 2013 next to Gyeongbokgung, designed by mpART Architects (Min Hyun-jun). The museum itself was founded in 1969 as the country's only national art museum dedicated to Korean modern and contemporary art, and it now has four branches, in Gwacheon, Deoksugung, Seoul and Cheongju. The Seoul building stands on and beside the site of the former Military Defense Security Command building. Its central idea is the madang, or yard, used to tie the building's interior and exterior to the surrounding city. These open yards also serve as public leisure space and as places for outdoor art events and programmes. Inside, Korean modern art is shown alongside an integrated programme of contemporary art.

Completed in 1987, the Paustian House in Copenhagen is one of Jørn Utzon's most significant works in Denmark. Utzon conceived the design and sent sketches to his sons Jan and Kim, who produced the final drawings and construction plans. The idea came from walking in a Danish beech forest, which Utzon likened to a hall of pillars that dissolves into branches and a leafy crown; the roof stands for that crown. From outside, the building has a temple-like look, with external pillars framing it along the harbour's edge. Inside, tall white columns with fan-shaped tops rise to the ceiling, where geometric archways join them. Kim Utzon later added two adjacent buildings, completed in 2000. For students it is a clear example of an image from nature carried directly into structure.

The Stadshal, or City Pavilion, is a large stand-alone canopy in the inner city of Ghent, Belgium, designed by Robbrecht en Daem with Marie-José Van Hee and built in 2012. It formed part of a wider city project to redevelop the squares and public spaces of Ghent's historic centre. The canopy stands on the square between three historic landmarks: the Belfry, the Renaissance Town Hall and St. Nicholas' Church. When it was built it drew criticism for its size, for its height and for bringing modern materials into such historic surroundings. That debate is the reason to study it. The project is a direct case for discussing how strongly a new structure should assert itself among old ones, and what a freestanding public roof brings to a square in the heart of a historic city.

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed the Barcelona Pavilion as the German Pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition. It was meant to present the new Weimar Germany as democratic, culturally progressive, prosperous and pacifist, a self-portrait in architecture. Because it held no exhibits, Mies could treat it as one continuous space that blurs inside and outside. Structure and enclosure are kept strictly apart: a regular grid of chrome-clad cruciform steel columns carries relatively small roof plates, while freely placed planes shape the space. Visitors are not led in a straight line but keep turning as they move through. The form is simple, the materials costly: marble, red onyx and travertine. Between 1983 and 1986 Catalan architects rebuilt it permanently, using historical drawings and footings rediscovered on the site.

Castelvecchio Museum in Verona, northern Italy, occupies the medieval castle whose name it shares. Between 1959 and 1973 Carlo Scarpa restored the building, and his hand shows in the details: doorways, staircases, furnishings and even fixtures made to hold one particular artwork. The renovation balances new and old with care, revealing the history of the original building where that was appropriate. The approach was unusual at the time but has since become common in renovation work, which is why the project matters to anyone learning how to work within historic buildings. The collection on display covers sculpture, statues, paintings, ancient weapons, ceramics, gold works, miniatures and some old bells, so the restored rooms and Scarpa's fittings had to suit a very wide range of objects.

Dudhsagar Dairy, officially the Mehsana District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union Limited, is a cooperative dairy union based in Mehsana, Gujarat. Its plant, designed by Achyut Kanvinde, is described as a postmodernist brutalist building; it was commissioned in 1970 and completed in 1973. The dairy grew from a cooperative movement in Mehsana, on the lines of the Amul model, that organised rural milk producers to pool their resources. The union was registered on 8 November 1960, and its foundation stone was laid on 2 April 1963. It has played a significant part in India's White Revolution and in rural development through the cooperative movement. For students, the plant is a case of an industrial building made for a farmers' cooperative, tying architecture to a wider social and economic programme.

Ammar Khammash built Feynan Ecolodge in 2005 in Wadi Feynan, at the western edge of Jordan's Dana Biosphere Reserve. Owned by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature, it was the first lodge of its kind in Jordan, developed to give local communities economic opportunities and to raise money for conserving the country's wild places. It also offers a sustainable alternative to open cast copper mining, which in Wadi Feynan is no longer viable and harms the environment. The lodge takes the shape of an ancient caravanserai. Solar panels power only the reception office, bathrooms and kitchen; the rest is lit by candles made locally by hand. Water comes from local springs, the vegetarian food is sourced within 40 km, and only local people work there, including local women, which is unusual in rural Jordan.

On the Islands Brygge waterfront in Copenhagen, MVRDV turned two seed silos built in 1963 into the Gemini Residence, converting them between 2002 and 2005. The name refers to the twin silos through Gemini, the zodiac sign of the Twins. The architects used the silos' hollow cores for stairs, lifts and hallways, and clipped the apartments onto the outside, each with floor-to-ceiling windows and balconies along its whole length. The two silos are joined on every floor, giving a plan like the infinity symbol. A Texlon roof over the two rotundas brings in daylight and creates a lobby as tall as the building. At the base the raw concrete is left bare to show the structure's history, and the overhang leaves a narrow passage between dockside and streetside.

Kala Academy is a cultural centre at Campal in Panjim, Goa, in a building by Charles Correa dating from 1983. The Government of Goa established the academy on 28 February 1970 as the apex body for promoting music, dance, drama, fine art, folk art and literature. Correa's complex brings several kinds of space for these arts together in one place: an auditorium, an amphitheatre, a black box theatre, an art gallery and a library. Beyond performance and display, the academy trains students through its faculty and runs festivals, competitions, exhibitions, workshops and seminars on the local arts. Its future is now uncertain. The Goa government has said the structure could not be repaired or renovated and might have to be demolished, which makes it an urgent case in the debate over keeping or replacing modern buildings.

This parking garage in the South Beach area of Miami Beach was designed by the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron and stands at the western end of the Lincoln Road Mall, where it meets Alton Road. The developer, Robert Wennett, wanted to revive that end of the mall; he kept the existing building and added a garage of equal height beside it, choosing the architects after interviewing ten well-known firms. The design, led by partner Christine Binswanger, has been likened to a house of cards: an open-air frame with no exterior walls, built from buttresses and cantilevers, with floor heights from 8 to 34 feet. Some ramps are steep to bridge the taller levels, and lifts and a central winding stair take drivers to and from their cars. It has become a destination for architects and photographers.

Le Corbusier designed La Cité de Refuge in Paris for the Salvation Army, his third building for the organisation, and it was built from 1929 to 1933 at 12 rue Cantagrel in the 13th arrondissement. It was one of his first urban housing projects. The plan sets a single long slab of cellular rooms at an angle to the street, fronted by free-standing sculptural volumes that hold the shared rooms: reception hall, dining room and offices. The facade was designed as a sealed glass wall with forced air ventilation, but the system never worked properly and was hard to control. Pierre Jeanneret later oversaw repairs, the addition of a brise soleil between 1948 and 1952 and new windows for the roof pavilions. Listed as a National Historical Monument of France in 1975, it was renovated from 2007 to 2016.

The Cranbrook Estate in Bethnal Green, London, was designed by Francis Skinner and Douglas Bailey with their elder mentor Berthold Lubetkin, who had pioneered modernist design in Britain in the 1930s. The estate replaced terraced houses, workshops and a large factory with a figure-of-eight street, Mace Street, which echoes the diagonal street pattern to the north. Along it stand six tower blocks, set in pairs in order of height. They opened in 1963 and were named after the towns and boroughs that Bethnal Green was twinned with at the time: Alzette, Mödling, Offenbach, Puteaux, St Gilles and Velletri. Residents have kept shaping the place since. In 2009 they turned a run-down children's playground into the Cranbrook Community Food Garden, which grows fresh vegetables.

Philip Johnson and John Burgee designed this theater for ballet and dance at Lincoln Center in Manhattan, which opened on 23 April 1964 as the New York State Theater. The State of New York paid for it as part of its cultural role in the 1964–1965 World's Fair, and it has been home to the New York City Ballet ever since. The auditorium seats 2,586, with broad seating at orchestra level, four main balconies called Rings and a small Fifth Ring, under a gold latticed ceiling with a large spherical chandelier at its centre. In 2008 David H. Koch pledged $100 million over ten years for renovation and an endowment, and the theater took his name. The renovation added two aisles to the orchestra level, a new stage lighting system and a larger orchestra pit with a lift in its floor.

Oscar Niemeyer's Edifício Niemeyer is a residential building in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, built between 1954 and 1960 on a triangular lot at the corner of Praça da Liberdade and Avenida Brasil, where the Dolabela Palace once stood. Its curved form was inspired by the mountains around the city, and horizontal concrete brise-soleil run across it. The twelve storeys hold 22 apartments of different sizes and layouts. The open ground floor was meant to frame views of the Serra do Curral range behind the square, though later development has blocked them. The design was controversial at the time, as some objected to private homes on the public square. Completed before the works of Brasília, it was one of the first modernist buildings in Belo Horizonte, and it is now listed at municipal, state and federal levels.

Opened on 5 December 2008 in Yinzhou District, the Ningbo History Museum presents the history and traditional customs of the Ningbo area. Its architect, Wang Shu, became the first Chinese citizen to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2012. The concept combines mountains, water and oceans. The first three levels form a single square base with the main entrances and offices, while the galleries above fracture, like the nearby mountains, into five smaller sections of sharp geometric shapes. Stones and bricks salvaged from demolished buildings in the area were laid by builders, who were given some freedom, using the wapan technique; other walls carry cement-covered bamboo, with each wall's angle deciding its material. Reported as the first museum built with a large number of used materials, it won the Lu Ban Prize, China's top architecture award, in 2009.

Richard Meier's Stadthaus stands on the Münsterplatz, or Minster Square, in the centre of Ulm, Germany, and is used mainly for exhibitions of photography and modern and contemporary art. Meier set out both to complement and to contrast with the Gothic style of the Ulmer Münster. Construction began in 1991, after the elected council ruled against a narrow vote, and the building was finished in 1993. Its 3,600 square metres are spread over four levels joined by an open staircase, with views into the building and out beyond it. The materials answer the setting: Spanish Rosa Dante granite clads the building, floors the terraces and paves the square, while the incline of the roof reflects the neighbouring buildings. In 2019 it was listed as a monument of special significance to national heritage.

Churchill College is a constituent college of the University of Cambridge with a primary focus on science, engineering and technology. Its architects, Richard Sheppard, Robson & Partners, won a competition of 19 entrants, chosen from a shortlist of four by a panel that included Winston Churchill. Sheppard's firmly modernist scheme uses brown brick walls, precast concrete lintels and teak-framed glazing, softened by grounds laid out to Sheila Haywood's 1959 landscape master plan. By completion in 1968 there were nine main residential courts and a central building with the dining hall, buttery, combination rooms and offices. The chapel reads as a modern take on a Byzantine basilica: a Greek cross marked out in concrete beams and exposed brick, with eight narrow slit windows of stained glass designed by John Piper. The central buildings and chapel are each Grade II listed.

Built in phases between 1961 and 1971 in Pimlico, London, Lillington Gardens follows a plan by Darbourne & Darke and was among the last high-density public housing schemes of London's postwar period. Its central idea was to reach high density in a medium-rise structure rather than in towers. The estate stresses individuality in the way homes are grouped, with private gardens at both ground and roof level. Wide 'roof streets' with planted gardens, together with the high build quality, help it sit comfortably beside the surrounding Victorian terraces. The site wraps around the Grade I listed Church of St James the Less, built in 1859–61. In 1973 the historian Nikolaus Pevsner called it 'easily the most interesting recent housing in inner London', and it remains a strong reference for dense housing without towers.

Rem Koolhaas of OMA designed the Netherlands Embassy on Roland Ufer in Berlin-Mitte, beside the new government district; it opened in 2004. The brief asked for a solitary building that joined conventional civil service security with Dutch openness. OMA's answer mixes obedience and disobedience: the block's perimeter is completed, while the embassy itself rises as a freestanding cube. Diplomats had often met informally in the hallway of their old building, so the new one centres on a continuous route that climbs through all eight storeys. Offices are the 'leftover' spaces carved out by this route, placed along the facade, and part of it is a diagonal void that frames the TV Tower from the park. The route also serves as the main air duct, feeding fresh air to the offices. The design won the Mies van der Rohe Award for European Architecture in 2005.

In the Sendling-Westpark district of Munich, the ADAC Headquarters is a high-rise office building that Sauerbruch Hutton designed after winning first prize in the competition; it was built between 2006 and 2011. The scheme stacks two parts: a five-storey base with rounded edges, shaped like an amoeba, and 18 tower floors above it. Colour drives the design. The facade is made of 1,152 elements in 22 colours that read together like a mosaic, and the palette was taken mainly from the client's brand colour. Besides offices, the complex holds a visitor and conference centre, a casino, a printing works and a television studio. On the same site, the historic Sander Villa was renovated with its original facade largely restored, and it now houses the library, archive and a conference room.

Peter Behrens's best-known work, the AEG Turbine Factory went up in 1909 in Berlin's Moabit district. Behrens led the design with the engineer Karl Bernhard, and he had been working for AEG since 1907 as artistic consultant, shaping its products, logo and graphics. The building is seen as the first attempt to bring restrained modern design to industrial architecture. Along its 100-metre length, steel columns stand bare on the outside, bolts and joints exposed, with tall glass windows between them that lean slightly inward towards the top. The gable ends are reinforced concrete; metal strapping on the piers gives them a rusticated look, and the company logo is cast into the gable. Critics have called it a "temple of power" (David Watkin) and an up-to-date Parthenon (Tom Wilkinson). A century on, it still makes turbines.

Amos Rex is an independent, privately funded museum of contemporary art in Helsinki, named after the publisher and arts patron Amos Anderson. JKMM Architects placed it beneath Lasipalatsi Square on Mannerheimintie boulevard, and it opened in August 2018. The aim was to join new and old: the galleries go underground so that the historic Lasipalatsi building keeps its place above. Chief architect Asmo Jaaksi wanted some contact between street level and the world below, and the answer is a group of domes rising from the square. They act as art elements and as skylights, bringing daylight down into the museum. The New York Times compared the five conical domes to inverted craters bubbling up from the paving. Inside, the exhibition hall is shaped by ceiling discs that hide technical services and also help with acoustics and appearance.

Between Brunswick Square and Russell Square in Bloomsbury, London, the Brunswick Centre combines homes and shops in one grade II listed complex. Patrick Hodgkinson designed it in the mid-1960s, building on studies by Leslie Martin, and it replaced streets of run-down Georgian terraces. It began as a private scheme when private mixed-use development was rare in the UK. Built from 1967 to 1972, it fell short of its planned size. Hodgkinson meant the blocks to be painted cream, a Georgian colour, in homage to the terraces it replaced. With too few private buyers, the flats were leased to Camden as council housing, while the developer kept the structure and shops. Listed in 2000, it was renovated from November 2002, when the blocks got their planned colour and artist Susanna Heron added water features to the central space.

Named after Canadian National, the railway company that built it, the CN Tower is a communications and observation tower in downtown Toronto, completed in 1976. The idea dates from 1968, when CN wanted a large television and radio platform for the region that would also show the strength of Canadian industry. Reflective new skyscrapers were weakening signals, so taller antennas were needed. An early tripod of three cylindrical pillars evolved into a single hexagonal core with three legs that form a Y at ground level. The core rose on a hydraulic slipform, a platform that jacked itself upward as the concrete below set. Six elevators run in glass-lined shafts set into the three inner angles of the hexagon. It was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years, until the Burj Khalifa passed it in 2007.

In the Centro neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, the Petrobras Headquarters is a brutalist office building that the people who work there call Edise. It stands on Avenida República do Chile, beside the Metropolitan Cathedral. Roberto Luís Gandolfi's design was chosen through a national competition run by the Brazilian Institute of Architects, from more than 200 entries. The key move is the facade, whose spaces connect inside and outside while sheltering the offices from sun and heat. The building also has indoor and outdoor gardens by Roberto Burle Marx, and their original layout is listed by the city. In 2021 Edise was revitalised for the first time in nearly 50 years, with new measures for sustainability and inclusiveness, and the gardens are to be renewed on their original plan. It shows a brutalist facade doing real climatic work.

Andrew Melville Hall is a Category A listed student residence of the University of St Andrews in Fife, Scotland. James Stirling designed it in the New Brutalist style during the university's large expansion of the 1960s, and it was built from prefabricated concrete modules. It sits prominently on the North Haugh, along a ridge looking over the St Andrews Links, and its form is said to recall passing ships, a theme common in Stirling's work. The geometry carries through to the bedrooms, which have irregular octagonal plans. On top of some blocks, glass enclosures shaped like garden greenhouses bring daylight into the stairwells. Construction errors meant decades of repair work, and plans for more buildings of the same design were dropped. DoCoMoMo named it one of its Key Scottish Monuments in 1993, and it was listed Category A in 2011.

On the Wilhelminapier in Rotterdam, De Rotterdam is a skyscraper by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture that holds offices, a hotel and apartments. It is made of three linked towers rising from a shared six-floor base, whose lowest two levels form a large glass plinth. At about 90 metres up, each tower shifts a few metres in a different direction; this improves stability in the wind and makes room for terraces. In OMA's original design the towers stood apart, but they now touch in a few places to simplify the structural forces and keep construction affordable. The facade allows natural ventilation. OMA calls the idea a vertical city: functions are grouped in blocks, while different users cross paths at various points inside. It is a useful study in how stacking and shifting volumes can serve both structure and programme.

Tore Björnstad's Maison de Radio-Canada in Montréal was the broadcast headquarters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's French-language radio and television, with its studios and master control. Most of the working-class Faubourg à m'lasse neighbourhood was demolished to make room for it, and the last house was emptied on October 1, 1963. The old complex's address is 1400 René Lévesque Boulevard East, a street named after the former premier who once worked as a CBC reporter and commentator. The broadcaster moved to a new building at 1000 Papineau Avenue, inaugurated on September 7, 2022. By April 2025 most of the old buildings had been pulled down for a future residential project, and the redevelopment would reconnect the street grid that the 1960s clearance cut. It is a clear case study in large-scale clearance and later repair.

Manhattan House is a 21-storey apartment building at 200 East 66th Street on Manhattan's Upper East Side, built from 1949 to 1951. Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it with Mayer & Whittlesey, and New York Life developed it for middle-class residents. The plan is a central spine with five wings facing north and south, set back from both side streets. Older New York apartment blocks pushed their facades to the lot line and kept gardens inside; here the building pulls back and the gardens sit outside. It was among the first in the city to use pale white brick as its main facade material, glazed so rain would wash it clean, and many white-brick buildings followed. Robert A. M. Stern saw it as New York's most literal version of Le Corbusier's postwar idea of vertical living.

The Margaret Esherick House in Philadelphia is among the most studied of the nine houses Louis Kahn built. Margaret Esherick, who owned a bookstore in Chestnut Hill, commissioned it, and it was finished in 1961. From the street it reads as a flat-roofed rectangular block of stucco-faced concrete block, long side forward. Kahn often split buildings into served and servant spaces, and here four alternating strips, each two storeys high, run from front to back. In the double-height living room, a built-in bookcase fills most of the front wall, a nod to the client's trade, while her uncle, the craftsman Wharton Esherick, made the wood and copper kitchen. Every side has its own pattern of windows and ventilation. At the rear, large fixed panes sit between stacks of shutters that open in any combination to link inside and out.

Rising 157 metres over 35 floors beside the Bay of Montevideo, the Antel Tower is the tallest skyscraper in Uruguay. It holds the headquarters of ANTEL, the country's government-owned telecommunications company. The Uruguayan-Canadian architect Carlos Ott designed it, and American Bridge completed it in 2002 with other members of a design/build consortium. Its formal name is Torre de las Telecomunicaciones, and it is also called Torre Joaquín Torres García. The tower is the main part of a complex that also includes a Customer Service Building, a Telecommunications Museum and an Auditorium, with a total area of 19,459 square metres. Construction did not go smoothly: problems on site pushed the cost from an original $65 million to $102 million. It shows a national company grouping its headquarters, public services and a museum on one waterfront site.

On the Japanese island of Naoshima, Benesse House is both an art museum and a hotel, designed by Tadao Ando. The idea took shape in 1985 between Tetsuhiko Fukutake, founding president of Fukutake Publishing, and Naoshima's mayor, Chikatsugu Miyake. When it opened in 1992 it was an early step in turning the island into a haven for art. Facing the mountains of Shikoku, it is arranged in four hotel areas, called the Museum, the Park, the Beach and the Oval. Art continues outside, where a pumpkin by Yayoi Kusama sits by the ocean. Ando returned in 2022 with two new galleries: the Valley Gallery, between Benesse House and the Chichu Art Museum, and the Hiroshi Sugimoto Gallery, which extends the Park. In 2025 Travel + Leisure counted it among the first art hotels in the world.

In Elkins Park, near Philadelphia, Beth Sholom is a Conservative synagogue and the only Jewish house of worship that Frank Lloyd Wright designed. Rabbi Cohen wanted a modern building, but found the International Style too plain to show clearly that this was a Jewish place of worship. With his agreement, Wright turned the octagonal plan into a hexagon, and in 1954 presented a form loosely based on Mount Sinai. A base of glass, steel and reinforced concrete supports a tetrahedron-shaped roof. Its panels pair corrugated plastic inside with wire glass outside; the double layer cut glare, eased summer ventilation and absorbed heat in winter. The sanctuary has no columns, aisles, traditional pews or spires, and its floor slopes down toward the centre. Delays meant it was dedicated in September 1959, after Wright's death.

The Blue Condominium is an apartment building in the Exarcheia neighbourhood of Athens, on the corner of Arachovis and Themistokleous Streets beside Exarcheia Square. Kyriakos Panagiotakos designed it, and it was built for him in 1932–1933. It is seen as a very important example of modern architecture in the city. The nickname comes from the dark blue that first coloured its facade, a shade chosen by the painter Spyros Papaloukas. The block is in fact two independent six-floor buildings, joined at the top floor. Panagiotakos gave close attention to the shared spaces: two entry halls, concierge desks, corridors, staircases, a laundry and a meeting room on the top floor. A pool was part of the original plans but was never finished. Le Corbusier saw the building during the fourth CIAM congress and called it very beautiful.

Built from 1964 to 1966 as the third home of the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Breuer Building stands on Madison Avenue in New York. Marcel Breuer and Hamilton P. Smith were the main architects, with Paul Weidlinger as structural engineer. It was Breuer's first museum and is his only surviving work in Manhattan. The form is stark and angular, faced in variegated granite and exposed concrete. Its upper floors step out over the entrance like an inverted ziggurat, so the cantilevered front acts as a portico, with the space beneath lit at night. Breuer chose materials meant to weather and age well: coarse granite, split slate floors, bronze doors and fittings, and teak. Sources call it Brutalist or wider Modernist. Its design influenced later buildings including the Cleveland Museum of Art's north wing and Atlanta's Central Library.

The Church of the Light is the main chapel of the Ibaraki Kasugaoka Church in Ibaraki, Osaka Prefecture, built in 1989 and among Tadao Ando's most famous designs. It was planned as an addition to a wooden chapel and a minister's house already on the site. The building is a concrete volume of three 5.9-metre cubes, cut through by a wall set at 15 degrees that separates the chapel from the entrance area. Behind the altar, a cross is cut into the concrete wall, running floor to ceiling and wall to wall and lined up with the joints of the concrete; daylight enters through it. The benches and floorboards reuse scaffolding from the construction. Ando often draws on Zen thinking, and one theme here is the dual nature of existence. One opening in plain concrete shapes the whole room.

The Copan Building is a residential skyscraper at 200 Avenida Ipiranga in central São Paulo, inaugurated in 1966. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, with structural design by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, to celebrate the city's fourth centenary, and Niemeyer was personally responsible for its sinuous facade. The idea was a building open to a mixed cross-section of Brazilian society: its six blocks hold 1,160 apartments of varying sizes for an estimated five thousand residents, plus more than seventy businesses. The plan first included a second building, a hotel, but only the housing was built; the name is an acronym of the original developer, Companhia Pan-Americana de Hotéis e Turismo. At 115 metres and 32 floors, it has the largest reinforced concrete structure in Brazil. Since 2014 a transparent drape has wrapped it to protect pedestrians from loose mosaic tiles.

Belén Library Park is one of ten library parks in Medellín, Colombia, set in the city's Comuna 16, the Belén commune. Its design grew out of an academic exchange. In 2006, universities in Colombia began a sharing programme with the University of Tokyo, and as part of it a group of Tokyo architects led by the Japanese architect Hiroshi Naito donated the design of the library. The project dates from 2008 and joins the library to open public space. Its grounds are laid out as three different settings: a green plaza, a water plaza and a plaza for the public. For students, it is an example of a library planned together with its outdoor spaces, and of a public building shaped by collaboration between universities in two countries.

About 12 km from Paris, in Noisy-le-Grand, Les Espaces d'Abraxas is a high-density housing complex that Ricardo Bofill and his practice, Ricardo Bofill Taller de Arquitectura, designed in 1978 for the French government. Completed in 1982, it holds 591 apartments in three buildings: Le Palacio, the largest, Le Théâtre to its west, and the smaller L'Arc between them. The design is postmodern, using classical motifs and new building technology to give housing a luxury look once kept for the upper classes. Its facades are precast concrete panels, coloured by mixing oxides into the cement. The three blocks surround a grass-lined plaza modelled on the Roman Forums. That shared space was central for Bofill, who wanted the scheme to mix social categories and build community spirit. It shows classical form made by industrial means.

Hôtel van Eetvelde is a town house in Brussels that Victor Horta designed in Art Nouveau style for Edmond van Eetvelde, administrator of the Congo Free State. It was built between 1895 and 1898, and Horta added two extensions between 1898 and 1901. Its openly displayed steel and glass, materials then seen as industrial, were a novelty in prestigious private homes, and Horta also used a hanging steel construction for the facade. Inside, the central building revolves around an octagonal rotunda under a skylight, and a central reception room covered by a stained glass cupola brings extra light into the house. The rotunda works as a small winter garden, ringed by circulation that links the living room, dining room and stairwell. In 2000 it joined three other Horta town houses on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Known in Paris as the maison ronde, or round house, the Maison de la Radio is the headquarters of Radio France. Henry Bernard was chosen from 26 entrants, and the building was completed in 1963. It takes the form of a huge ring, 500 metres around, with a central utility tower, and holds offices, broadcasting studios and performance spaces for its stations and four permanent ensembles. The site, first a gasworks and then a stadium, suited the purpose because it was close to the Eiffel Tower and its radio transmitters. In 2005 a major renovation was awarded to Architecture-Studio, with acoustics by Nagata Acoustics. Inside, walls and balcony fronts are clad in faceted panels of birch, beech and cherry, and an 852-seat hall has been known for its fine acoustics since 1963. Godard used the building in his film Alphaville.

The Norwegian Glacier Museum, or Norsk Bremuseum, stands in Fjærland, in Vestland county, Norway, and was designed by the architect Sverre Fehn; it dates from 1991. Its stated purpose is to collect, create and share knowledge about glaciers and climate, and it gives visitors information about the Jostedalsbreen glacier and Jostedalsbreen National Park. Fehn stayed with the building as it grew. In 2002 the decision was taken to extend the museum, again to his design, and the Ulltveit-Moe Climate Centre, another Fehn addition, opened within it in 2007. For students, the museum is a chance to follow one architect's work on a single building over many years, from the first design through its later additions, and to look at a public building devoted to explaining glaciers and climate.

Behind the American Italian Cultural Center in downtown New Orleans, the Piazza d'Italia is a public plaza completed in 1978 to a design by Charles Moore with Perez Architects. In the early 1970s, leaders of the city's Italian-American community wanted a permanent public tribute to the Italian immigrant experience. Moore's answer is a fountain shaped like the Italian peninsula, ringed by curved colonnades, a clock tower, and a campanile and Roman temple drawn as abstract space frames. Classical forms and orders are treated playfully, built in stainless steel and neon, with jets of water suggesting the acanthus leaves of Corinthian capitals. Praised at its debut, the development planned around it was never built, and the plaza decayed. It was fully restored by 2004, alongside the neighbouring Lykes Center's conversion into a hotel.

The Sapporo Dome is a stadium in Sapporo, Hokkaido, used mainly for association football, which opened in 2001 with 41,580 seats. Hiroshi Hara's building switches between two entirely different surfaces. Baseball is played on an artificial turf field, while football uses a grass pitch that slides into and out of the stadium as needed. A change from baseball to football begins by storing the artificial turf. Several stadiums elsewhere have sliding pitches, but unlike most of them, Sapporo's sits under a fixed roof. The hovering system used to convert the turf also helped make snow in 2007, when the Dome became the first venue at world championship or Winter Olympic level to host indoor, night-time skiing events, including cross-country sprints. It is a useful study in designing one large hall around changing uses.

Set 130 metres inside a sandstone mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, in the Arctic Svalbard archipelago, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a secure backup for the world's crop diversity. Designed by Peter W. Soderman, it stores duplicate seeds from gene banks around the world. It officially opened on 26 February 2008, with the first seeds arriving the month before. The roof and entrance are filled with highly reflective stainless steel, mirrors and prisms, and an illuminated artwork by Dyveke Sanne, Perpetual Repercussion, runs along the roof and down the front face to mark the site from a distance. The vault also has robust security systems. When warm weather and heavy rain in October 2016 pushed water into the entrance, the design ensured it froze within a few metres, and the seeds were never at risk.

Vladimir Shukhov designed the Adziogol Lighthouse in 1910 and built it in 1911. It is one of two active lighthouses in Ukraine's Dnieper Estuary made as vertical lattice hyperboloids of steel bars. The tower stands on a concrete pier on a tiny islet in the combined Dnieper-Bug Estuary, about 2.5 km north of the village of Rybalche, and takes its name from the Cape of Adzhyhol to its north. The site can be reached only by boat. Working together with the Stanislav Range Front Light, it serves as a range light, guiding ships entering the Dnieper River or the Southern Buh River. On 22 July 2022 it was damaged in a Russian missile attack, when three rockets hit it. For students, it is a working example of Shukhov's hyperboloid steel lattice.

The Modern Wing of the Art Institute of Chicago, designed by Renzo Piano, opened on 16 May 2009 as the largest expansion in the museum's history, bringing its footprint to nearly one million square feet. It houses the museum's early 20th-century European art, including Picasso's The Old Guitarist, Matisse's Bathers by a River and Magritte's Time Transfixed. A key part of Piano's design is its window screening, which protects the art from direct sunlight; a gallery he designed alongside the wing uses the same screening. The wing won at the Chicago Innovation Awards in 2009 and drove a rise in visitor numbers even after admission fees went up by 25 percent. In 2010 the museum sued the engineering firm Ove Arup over what it said were flaws in the concrete floors and air-circulation systems. It is a case study in gallery daylight.

Raj Rewal designed the Asian Games Village in New Delhi as the athletes' village for the 1982 Asian Games. It stands on the remains of the Khalji dynasty's Siri Fort and later became a residential colony. The complex has 700 housing units: 200 individual houses and 500 apartments in blocks of two to four storeys. Its order comes from a hierarchy of courtyards at different levels. Streets are narrow and shaded, broken into small units that create pauses and places to rest. Terraces give semi-private outdoor space and recall the houses of Jaisalmer. Cars and pedestrians are kept apart but closely linked: peripheral roads lead to cul-de-sac parking areas, which give access to garages or car porches beside each home. It is a strong precedent for low-rise housing ordered by courtyards and shaded lanes.

The Aula Magna is an auditorium at the Central University of Venezuela, in the University City of Caracas, next to the main library. Carlos Raúl Villanueva designed it in the 1940s, and the Danish firm Christiani & Nielsen built it under a contract that allowed only four months, from 28 November 1952 to 31 March 1953. It was the main building of Villanueva's Synthesis of the Arts project for the campus. He described his buildings not as objects but as "movements", and this was the fourth. Its defining feature is the acoustic clouds, Alexander Calder's 1953 Floating Clouds, which join technology and art and serve both looks and sound. Calder's panels were not first meant for the interior of the hall. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in November 2000 for its artistic and architectural significance.

Built in 1857 in Kashan, Iran, the Borujerdi House is now a historic house museum. Ustad Ali Maryam designed it for the bride of the wealthy merchant Borujerdi; her family, the Tabātabāei, had already commissioned the nearby Tabatabai House from the same architect. The plan follows the traditional Iranian split between the biruni, the public area, and the andaruni, the private quarters, with a courtyard, a fountain pool and a two-storey iwan. A central dome, or khishkhan, crowns the main hall. Three windcatchers, each about 40 metres tall, stand on the house, two above the main hall and one over the entrance. Inside, stucco, glass work and ayeneh-kari sit alongside frescoes by the painter Kamal-ol-Molk. For students, it shows the public and private halves of a traditional Iranian house in one compact example.

The Frederic C. Hamilton Building is an expansion of the Denver Art Museum, designed as a joint venture by Studio Daniel Libeskind and Davis Partnership Architects, the architect of record. Clad in glass and titanium, it opened on 7 October 2006 and was Libeskind's first completed building in the United States. Its sharp angles echo the nearby Rocky Mountains and the geometric crystals found at their base, and Libeskind said the light and geology of the Rockies inspired him. Inside are the museum's Modern and Contemporary, African and Oceanic Art collections, plus special exhibition spaces. A bridge pavilion connected it to the 1971 North Building by Gio Ponti, now the Martin Building. Its unusual steel configuration won an AISC Presidential Award of Excellence in 2007, and the American Institute of Architects recognised it as a successful Building Information Modeling project.

On Frankfurt's Museumsufer, the Deutsches Architekturmuseum occupies an 18th-century building whose interior Oswald Mathias Ungers redesigned in 1984. His concept was a set of 'elemental Platonic buildings within elemental Platonic buildings', a nesting of pure forms inside the historic shell. The permanent exhibition, 'From Ancient Huts to Skyscrapers', traces how architecture developed in Germany, while several temporary shows, conferences, symposia and lectures run each year. The collection holds about 180,000 architectural drawings and 600 models, including work by Erich Mendelsohn, Mies van der Rohe, Archigram and Frank O. Gehry. For students, the building is a lesson in setting a new interior order inside an older structure, and the museum is a major resource for seeing how architects draw and model their ideas.

Sean Godsell designed Kew House as his own family home, built in 1996–1997 in the Melbourne suburb of Kew, Victoria. It is a minimalist glass box, 18 by 9 metres, wrapped on two sides by rusted metal screens and cantilevered 5.5 metres over a steep slope. Godsell calls it elemental rather than processed: rust, oiled second-hand boards and recycled decking take the place of precious detail. The Japanese-influenced plan has no corridors; space flows on, divided only by the kitchen and bathroom, a long central wall holding a fireplace and cupboards, and sliding screens. The screens on the north and west keep summer sun off the windows, and sections lift so winter sun can warm the living spaces. The 2000 International Architecture Year Book read the house as a speculation on an Australian vernacular that blends east and west.

The Seattle Art Museum created and runs the Olympic Sculpture Park, a free public park for modern and contemporary sculpture in downtown Seattle, opened in January 2007. Weiss/Manfredi Architects led the design with Charles Anderson Landscape Architecture and Magnusson Klemencic Associates. The land was an oil and gas industrial site that became a contaminated brownfield before the museum turned it into one of downtown's rare green spaces. The park combines a 9-acre outdoor sculpture museum, an indoor pavilion and a beach on Puget Sound. At the water's edge, a three-level underwater slope of riprap was built, its lower level designed to draw sea life and kelp. Permanent pieces, temporary works and site-specific installations share the grounds, though the salt air corrodes exposed wood and metal and makes upkeep expensive. It shows how a polluted industrial edge can become public landscape.

Tel Aviv City Hall is the city's municipal government centre, holding the mayor's office, meeting chambers and council offices. Menachem Cohen designed it in the 1950s in the Brutalist style. Before it, the municipality sat on Rothschild Boulevard and later used a hotel on Bialik Street as it needed more space; in 1972 the old Skora building became a museum of the city's history. At the foot of the new building lies a large plaza, designed as a central place for public events and ceremonies. First called Kings of Israel Square, it was renamed Rabin Square in 1995 after Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated there. The building is often lit with other countries' flags to show solidarity after disasters and attacks. For students, it pairs a Brutalist civic block with the public square laid out at its base.

On the corner of Portland Place and Weymouth Street in Marylebone, London, 66 Portland Place is the headquarters of the Royal Institute of British Architects. RIBA had been based at 9 Conduit Street since 1859 and outgrew it, so in 1929 it announced a design competition. The contest drew 284 entries, a high number for a fairly modest building, and George Grey Wornum won it. King George V and Queen Mary opened the building on 8 November 1934. Its style is mainly Art Deco blended with late neoclassical, also called Imperial Neoclassical after the work of Sir Edwin Lutyens and Sir Herbert Baker. Outside, the Deco character shows in the bronze doors, the architectural motifs and a main window that runs through more than one storey. It was listed grade II* in 1970, thirty-seven years after it was built.

Aula Magna is the largest auditorium at Stockholm University, completed in 1998 and used for events that include Nobel lectures. Ralph Erskine designed it as his last project for the university. The building is set into the ground, so it looks low and modest from the north, where it is faced in red brick, while the south side opens up with full-height glass. Erskine broke the facade into many volumes of different size and height. On the roof, sun reflectors typical of his work send daylight through skylights into the auditorium. Inside, exposed bedrock in the lower foyer and blonde wood lining give a natural feel against the glass and stone. The plan of the hall follows the semi-circle of an ancient amphitheatre. It is a good case of bringing daylight into a large hall from above.

The Bode Museum stands on Museum Island in the historic centre of Berlin, built between 1898 and 1904 to plans by Ernst von Ihne in a Baroque Revival style. It opened as the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, named after Emperor Frederick III, and in 1956 took the name of its first curator, Wilhelm von Bode. During the Second World War part of the collection was kept in the Flakturm Friedrichshain, an anti-aircraft tower, and fires in 1945 destroyed some holdings. The museum closed for repairs in 1997 and reopened on 18 October 2006 after a €156 million refurbishment. In keeping with Bode's belief in mixing art collections, it now shows sculpture, Byzantine art, and coins and medals. As part of Museum Island, it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999 for its architecture and as evidence of how museums developed as a cultural phenomenon.

Giovanni Michelucci's church of San Giovanni Battista stands in Campi Bisenzio, near Florence, inside a large rest area shared by two motorways. Its position between the Autostrada del Sole and the A11 Firenze-Mare highway earned it the name Church of the Freeway of the Sun, though it is formally dedicated to John the Baptist. Built between 1960 and 1963, it sets out to reflect both modern and traditional church design: a cross plan and stone facing meet tent-like vertical elements and copper roofing. The walls are stone and concrete, and the copper roof has oxidised green outside while staying burnished blond inside, where marble, glass and bronze also appear. The asymmetrical plan follows sinuous curves, giving a sense of fluid space. Students can study how it keeps a traditional cross plan while letting the interior flow in curves.

Churchill Gardens is a large housing estate in Pimlico, Westminster, developed by Powell & Moya between 1946 and 1962 to replace Victorian terraces damaged in the Blitz. With 1,600 homes in 32 blocks, it is the only housing project completed under the Abercrombie Plan for redeveloping London. Tall slabs are enclosed by seven-storey blocks and interspersed with maisonettes and terraces, a pioneering example of mixed development that became a model for many later public housing schemes. Many of the tall blocks have lifts opening straight onto the street, with a local lift serving every floor and an express lift stopping only at every third. The estate also had an early district heating system, using heat from Battersea Power Station collected in a glass-faced accumulator tower. Its landscape is Grade II listed, and several buildings are listed individually.

Santiago Calatrava and Félix Candela designed the City of Arts and Sciences, a cultural and architectural complex in Valencia, Spain. It occupies the southeast end of the old Turia riverbed, which was drained and rerouted after a catastrophic flood in 1957 and turned into a sunken park. Work began in July 1996, and the complex was inaugurated on 16 April 1998 with the opening of L'Hemisfèric, an IMAX cinema, planetarium and laserium shaped like a giant eye. Its eyelid opens onto the surrounding pool: long aluminium awnings fold upward together to form a brise-soleil roof along the curved axis of the eye. L'Umbracle, an open structure over a landscaped walk planted with species native to Valencia, serves as the entrance. Budgeted in 1991 for three structures, the project grew, and the added buildings helped triple its cost.

The Des Moines Art Center in Iowa grew in three stages, each by a different architect, which lets students compare three approaches on one site. Construction started in 1945, and Eliel Saarinen's original wing, combining Art Nouveau and Art Deco styles, opened in 1948. I. M. Pei added a second wing in a Modernist style, designed in 1966 for large-scale sculpture and completed in 1968. Richard Meier's third wing followed in 1985, designed to let in as much natural ambient light as possible.
