The museum holds an extensive collection of paintings, sculpture, modern art and mixed media, and since 2009 it has also run the Pappajohn Sculpture Park in Western Gateway Park downtown. Seen together, the three wings trace the museum's growth from its opening to the mid-1980s.

The Design Museum in Kensington, London, exhibits product, industrial, graphic, fashion and architectural design. It began in a former 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the Thames at Shad Thames, altered to resemble an International Modernist building. In 2016 it moved into the former Commonwealth Institute, a Grade II* listed 1960s building by Robert Matthew, Johnson-Marshall and Partners that had stood vacant for over a decade. A design team led by John Pawson carried out the conversion, helped by a £17.5 million donation from Sir Terence Conran, and the museum opened there on 24 November 2016. From the atrium, a main staircase reaches every floor and gives views up to the hyperbolic paraboloid roof. Beneath that roof, the top floor holds a permanent display of key objects from the collection. It is a clear case of giving a listed modern building a new use.

In Beitou Park, within Taipei's Beitou District, the Beitou branch of the Taipei Public Library opened in November 2006 and is known as Taiwan's first green library. Bio-architecture Formosana designed the two-storey building with one main aim: to curb its consumption of water and electricity. Large windows bring in daylight and reduce the power needed for lighting. The roof does two jobs. It is partly covered with photovoltaic cells that generate electricity, and it captures rainwater, which is stored and then used to flush the toilets. For students, the library is a compact public building in which the energy and water strategy is the central design idea, and each measure is tied to a single, visible part of the building: the windows for light, the roof for power and water.

Bevin Court is a housing project in Finsbury, London, by the Tecton practice led by Berthold Lubetkin, completed in 1954 by Lubetkin with Francis Skinner and Douglas Carr Bailey. It stands on the site of Holford Square, destroyed by bombing, with the smaller Holford House and Amwell House beside the main block. The group reflects Lubetkin's respect for the existing city, a trait that sets his work apart from many modernists of his generation. Post-war austerity imposed tighter budgets than at Tecton's Spa Green Estate, forcing him to drop the planned balconies, community centre and nursery school. Instead he put his energy into the social space, creating a constructivist staircase at the heart of the building, described as a social condenser. Listed grade II* in December 1998, it was restored by the London Borough of Islington in 2014–2016.

The Muryangsujeon is the main hall of Buseoksa, a Buddhist temple near the mountain Bonghwangsan in Yeongju, South Korea, founded by the monk Uisang in 676. Re-constructed in 1376, it is the second oldest standing wooden building in the country and one of the few buildings from the Goryeo era that remain. The hall stands at the highest level of the temple and enshrines Amitabha. Stained paper found in 1916 recorded that it had been rebuilt in the early Goryeo years and that an enemy had set fire to it in 1358. The temple occupies a steep mountain site, and Koreans regard the ability to harmonise building and nature as the essence of architecture. For students, it is a rare surviving precedent of early Korean timber construction, placed with care on its slope.

Castello di Rivoli, near Turin, was once a residence of the Royal House of Savoy and now houses a museum of contemporary art. The castle was probably built in the 9th or 10th century and is first mentioned in 1159. In 1716 Filippo Juvarra planned a grandiose project, but only the two eastern wings were finished, leaving the facade incomplete. The building was heavily damaged in the Second World War and stayed largely abandoned until restoration began in 1979. The Turin architect Andrea Bruno carried out the first post-war renovation. In 1997 it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List together with 13 other Savoy residences. For students, it is a layered case: an unfinished Baroque scheme on a much older castle, restored after decades of neglect and given a new public use.

At the summit of Cerro Ávila in Caracas, 2,140 metres above sea level, Tomás Sanabria's Hotel Humboldt was built between May and November 1956. It formed part of a plan to link Caracas with the coast through a tourism and recreation complex that used the cable car for transport. The design centres on a cylindrical tower with 360° views, along with a restaurant, an observation deck and a private cable car. The glass and aluminium facade helped heat the building, and tilting windows allowed routine cleaning from the inside. A later restoration, led by the architect Gregory Vertullo, reinforced beams and columns with carbon fibre, and the adjoining Salón Boîte was restored to its original wall-covering patterns and carpet colour. The hotel is a case of a building conceived together with transport infrastructure to open a mountain summit to visitors.

Josef Gočár designed the House of the Black Madonna in Prague's Old Town in mid-1911, at the age of 31, as a department store for the wholesale merchant František Josef Herbst. Completed in 1912, it is the earliest example of cubist architecture in Prague and takes its name from a baroque Black Madonna sculpture kept from an earlier building on the site. Because of its central location, strict harmonisation rules required that it not clash with its historic setting, so Gočár drew on baroque forms. A reinforced-concrete skeleton allowed large interior spaces without ceiling supports, which suited the Cubist aesthetic. After years of alteration and damage, it was fully restored in 2003. A café now fills the first floor and the upper floors hold the Museum of Czech Cubism. It shows how a new style can work within rules set by a historic city centre.

On the shore of Lake Pampulha in Belo Horizonte, the Iate Tênis Clube is a recreational club designed by Oscar Niemeyer in the early 1940s. First called the Iate Golfe Clube, it is one of four buildings that Juscelino Kubitschek, then mayor, commissioned from Niemeyer when the dam that formed the lake was created. The main building has the Portinari Room on its upper level, named after Candido Portinari, who painted one of the murals on site, while the ground level shelters boats. Roberto Burle Marx designed the gardens. A 1970s annex with a party hall and gym was not by Niemeyer and differs in style, and UNESCO raised reservations about it. In 2016 the Pampulha ensemble became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, so the club is best studied together with its three companion buildings.

Kisho Kurokawa's Nagoya City Art Museum stands in Shirakawa Park in Nagoya, on a long triangular site surrounded by trees. Planning dates to the 1977 Nagoya City Basic Plan, which called for an art museum; construction began in 1985, the main building was finished in 1987, and the museum opened on 22 April 1988. Kurokawa kept the building below the height of the trees, placing the permanent galleries and storage underground. A sunken garden brings natural light into the approach to these lower galleries. The plan is organised along a north–south main axis, with a secondary axis opening to the northwest. According to the museum, the building also draws on Japanese traditional forms and local motifs. It is a useful study in keeping a public building low within a park while still bringing daylight to its underground rooms.

OCBC Centre is a skyscraper in Singapore and the headquarters of OCBC Bank. Designed by I. M. Pei, it is a prominent example of Brutalist architecture, a style popular in the 1960s and 1970s. The 52-storey tower rises 197.7 metres and was inaugurated on 1 October 1976, when it was the second-tallest building in Singapore and in South East Asia. The tower also has an unexpected tenant: in April 2024 a pair of Indo-Pacific peregrine falcons laid eggs on a concrete recess, the first time the species had done so in Singapore, and a tray of loose gravel was later installed as a nesting site. For students, it is a clear example of Pei working in the Brutalist idiom, and of a 1970s bank headquarters tower in South East Asia.

Facing the Trocadéro in Paris's 16th arrondissement, the Palais de Tokyo is a building dedicated to modern and contemporary art. André Aubert, Marcel Dastugue and Paul Viard designed it, and it takes its name from the street beside it, once called Avenue de Tokio. President Lebrun inaugurated it on 24 May 1937 during the International Exposition of Art and Technology in Modern Life, when it opened as the Palais des Musées d'art moderne. The building has two wings: the eastern one belongs to the city and the western one to the state. Since March 2002 the western wing has held a contemporary art centre, the largest museum in France for temporary exhibitions of contemporary art. In 2012 Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal overhauled and expanded it, before they went on to win the Pritzker Prize.

The parc de la Villette, the third-largest park in Paris at 55.5 hectares, lies on the city's northeastern edge in the 19th arrondissement. Bernard Tschumi won the design competition in 1982–83 as part of François Mitterrand's Grands Projets, and consulted the philosopher Jacques Derrida while preparing his proposal. Working with Colin Fournier, he built the park from 1984 to 1987 on the site of the city's huge abattoirs and national wholesale meat market. The park is meant to draw on the ideas of deconstructivism. Architectural follies, themed gardens and open spaces sit among museums, concert halls and theatres by several noted architects, including Christian de Portzamparc and Adrien Fainsilber, giving it one of the largest concentrations of cultural venues in Paris. It aims to appeal to adults and children alike, and for students it is a built test of deconstructivist ideas at the scale of a city park.

The Paul Löbe House is an office building of the German Bundestag in Berlin's government district, at the southern edge of Spreebogenpark. It belongs to the 'Band des Bundes' master plan by Schultes and Frank, which won an urban design competition for the Spreebogen area announced in 1992. In a further competition in 1994, the Munich architect Stephan Braunfels won with his design for both the Paul Löbe and Marie-Elisabeth Lüders Houses. The two form a unit: their roof edges share contours that follow the Spree, and two bridges join them across the river, which the architect calls a 'leap over the Spree'. Running east to west, the link symbolises the unity of East and West Germany and overrides the Nazi-era vision of a north–south axis. Inside, a spacious central hall cuts through the whole building, and courtyards carry art-in-architecture works.

The Tempodrom is a multi-purpose event venue in Berlin. Irene Moessinger founded it in 1980 in a large circus tent beside the Berlin Wall, on the west side of Potsdamer Platz. In 2001 it gained a permanent home on the site of the old Anhalter Bahnhof, whose war-damaged ruins had been demolished in 1960, and a small section of the station facade was kept. The firm gmp (von Gerkan, Marg and Partners) designed the new building on a square plan that holds three performance spaces. Two of these arenas are circular, and the larger, central one is covered by a 37-metre steel-and-concrete-panel roof meant to echo the tents of the original venue. For students, it is a clear case of a permanent building carrying the memory of a temporary one, on a site with its own layered history.

Astley Castle in North Warwickshire is a moated, fortified manor house rebuilt by the Grey family in 1555; most of what survives dates from then or later. Grade II* listed since 1952, it was severely damaged by fire in 1978 while in use as a hotel, then stood derelict as an official Building at Risk. In the early 2000s the owners, English Heritage, the local authority and the Landmark Trust planned its restoration. Witherford Watson Mann Architects, with engineers Mann Williams and Price & Myers, set modern elements within the mostly Renaissance remains, and the castle reopened as a holiday let in 2012. In 2013 it won the RIBA Stirling Prize as an exceptional example of blending an ancient monument with modern architecture. It is a strong precedent for any student working on new design inside a ruin.

The BMW Headquarters in Munich, also called the BMW Tower, has been the company's global headquarters since 1973. Built between 1968 and 1972 next to the Olympiapark, it was ready in time for the 1972 Summer Olympics. Karl Schwanzer designed both the tower and the BMW Museum, and together they evoke a car engine: four cylinders for the tower, with the museum as the cylinder head. The tower is made of four vertical cylinders, each divided horizontally at its centre by a mould in the facade. The cylinders do not stand on the ground; they hang from a central support tower. During construction, floors were assembled at ground level and then raised into position. Protected as a historic building in 1999, it is a clear example of a suspended structure in a high-rise.

Casals Hall in Ochanomizu, Tokyo, is a concert hall named in honour of the cellist Pau Casals. Designed by Arata Isozaki, with acoustic design by Nagata Acoustics, it opened in 1987 as a venue for chamber music. Its auditorium follows the shoebox form and seats 511. For the hall's tenth anniversary in 1997, a 41-stop organ by Jürgen Ahrend was installed. The publisher Shufunotomo Company originally owned and sponsored the hall, but economic conditions led to the withdrawal of funding in 2000. The university that later bought the building closed the hall in 2010, and a campaign to reopen it followed. For students, it is a compact study of the shoebox model for chamber music, and a reminder of how much a cultural building depends on lasting support.
